description: Hi, we're HealthLens, a group from the NASA Space Apps Irvine local hackathon. We chose Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts because, in the case of a Mars mission, there would be no physician around the corner, and it would be up to the astronauts to take care of their health issues. We blend software, AI, hardware design, and story telling to create things people will actually use.
summary: HealthLens is a visual health system that helps astronauts examine themselves and handle an emergency situation, as oftentimes there is no doctor on board and responses from Earth can take up to 44 minutes. The crew measures their vitals, blood glucose, sleep, mood, and symptoms, both manually and with the help of devices based on space station ones, passes eye and reaction tests, and takes pictures of their skin so an AI algorithm can detect any new or changing spots. Every measurement is compared with an individual baseline, and the status of every organ is colored in either green, amber, or red depending on how close it is to the baseline, which can be easily reviewed using a clickable 3D body. Every measurement comes with thorough instructions on why it’s important to track in space and what to do if something seems wrong. There is also an Emergency button that provides 15 step-by-step guides adapted to zero gravity and time lag based on NASA's Integrated Medical Model. HealthLens was designed based on NASA Human Research Program risks, OSDR spaceflight skin studies (OSD-238 to OSD-254), and live NASA DONKI space weather data.
details:
It’s halfway to Mars; a crewmate says they feel as if they’ve been stabbed in the chest and collapses. What do you do?

On a Mars mission, there is no doctor, and a question to Earth can take up to 44 minutes to answer, and a round trip alone exposes the crew to about 0.66 sieverts of radiation (Zeitlin et al., Science, 2013). HealthLens is the crew's own medic: a few minutes a day to check yourself, and clear steps when something doesn’t feel right.

What does it do?

  • Daily check-in in under a minute. Fifteen indicators: heart rate, blood pressure, blood oxygen, breathing rate, temperature, fasting blood sugar (mg/dL), body mass, sleep, mood, stress, fatigue, reaction time, skin spots, near vision, and the Amsler grid. Values are manually inputted or imported with one "Sync all" button, modeled on real space hardware: a smart shirt like the Canadian Space Agency's Bio-Monitor, a sleep wristband like the Actiwatch from NASA's Sleep-Long study, a body mass device like the ISS SLAMMD, and a finger-prick analyzer like CSA's Bio-Analyzer. (No hardware is connected in this prototype; imported values are labeled simulated.)
  • Tests that are built into the app. Weekly vision screening, as approximately 70% of space station astronauts have swelling at the back of their eyes (NASA, SANS), and a reaction time test, which may indicate considerable sleep deprivation before a crew member feels tired.
  • Skin scanning without missing any spots. The crew members are regularly taking photos of themselves, and the AI vision model detects all spots or even potentially dangerous malformations. HealthLens compares the results with the previous scan and evaluates if the spot is new or growing. Space radiation increases the risks of skin cancer, and additionally, skin diseases are among the most reported concerns on the ISS.
  • Daily symptom questionnaire. Chest pain, breathing problems, or fainting sound the alarm bell.
  • Instructions for non-medical specialists. All measurements include the explanation of how to do them, how they are important in space (linked to the five hazards of human spaceflight by NASA), what is the norm, what actions to take in case of deviation from the norm, and when to contact the flight surgeon.
  • Emergency mode. The red button on all screens opens 15 guides organized in three levels of priority based on the conditions found in NASA’s Integrated Medical Model: life-threatening (CPR, hypoxia, chest pain, anaphylaxis, smoky or toxic atmosphere, major bleeding), urgent (decompression syndrome, head trauma, hypoglycemia, syncope, radiation storm, ocular injury, extreme stress), and serious (burns, kidney stones). In case someone reports any chest pain or any dangerous condition, the corresponding guide will be offered to them first. All guides are executed on a step-by-step basis with a running timer, and the timed log is copied as a report for the baseline.
  • Designed based on the crew location. A mission bar provides information about the location of the crew (International Space Station, spacecraft on a route to Mars, Moon base, lunar rover, Mars base), gravity conditions, signal delay, and whether help will be available immediately or not. Depending on the location, body weight measurements, location to protect from radiation, important examinations and emergencies, and guidance: near Earth, "contact flight surgeon immediately"; on the way to Mars "send the report and continue; crew acts first".
  • 3-D Body Map. An actual anatomy model, either female or male, corresponding to each astronaut, with layers of skin, organs, and the skeleton. Each section is color-coded according to their condition and opens up its data, trend, and next actions.
  • Live NASA Space Weather. The NASA DONKI alerts turn into a radiation alert, which connects to the solar storms guide.
  • Notifications, streaks, and a flight surgeon’s report, summarizing observations, recommendations, and readings compared to baseline.

How does it work?

Each indicator is checked in four steps: 

(1) hard safety limits based on publicly available medical information, (2) difference relative to the baseline for the astronaut (first 7 measurements), (3) consistent pattern within the last 14 days, hence a slowly growing trend is detected before every measurement starts looking abnormal, and (4) overdue measurements. To prevent false alerts, a single unusual measurement requests a repeat measurement; the alert status is increased when the repeat measurement confirms the finding or when a hard safety limit is exceeded. The alert status for an astronaut is the maximum status out of all indicators, symptoms, and skin lesions. Skin lesions are evaluated according to the ABCDE rule recommended by dermatologists: the AI model evaluates the asymmetry, border, color, and size of the lesion; the app determines the OK, Watch, or Act status for the lesion and tracks each skin lesion independently of the others; moreover, the size of the lesion estimated only by the AI is not enough to trigger any alert on its own.

Worked example (demo crew, simulated data): Cmdr. Vega's spot on the left arm grew from 4 mm to 6.5 mm in 45 days with an irregular border, so she is at Act, and a report goes to the flight surgeon. Dr. Osei's blood pressure crept from about 121 to 134 mmHg in two weeks: Watch. Nakamura's heart rate and sleep drifted while every value still looked normal, and temperature checks were skipped: Watch. Lindqvist is healthy: OK.

What benefits does it have, and what is the intended impact?

The crew will receive one routine of several minutes per day, in simple language, with a clear guideline about the time of measurements. The flight surgeons will get a quick report without receiving an overwhelming amount of data, which is ready for transmission during the next communication session. Mission planners will receive one instrument from the space station to Mars. HealthLens can run offline, requires no additional equipment to operate, and accounts for the fact that the end user is not a doctor; thus, the same check-ins could be performed from a rural health center, an Antarctic research facility, or a vessel in the Pacific Ocean.

How is it creative?

  • It measures the astronaut’s change relative to their baseline rather than any fixed threshold level, spotting changes even if they are gradual.
  • It monitors every one of the astronaut’s skin lesions throughout the entire mission, as if a dermatologist were looking out for them.
  • The emergency responses are done step-by-step and modified for conditions in space (e.g., CPR while bracing against the wall, floating blood, water that doesn’t flow, distance from rescue), among others.
  • Location determines many things about the space mission, from weight measurement to potential emergencies.

What factors did we consider?

  • Astronauts are not doctors: all values have their own how, why, and what to do.
  • Distance from Earth: the app functions in offline mode, and its recommendations depend on the delay of the signal.
  • False alerts damage credibility, so the app measures again before escalating and comparing against individual baseline values.
  • Integrity of data: all values are accompanied by information on their origin (inputted, generated by devices, self-reported, measured within the app, simulated, or estimated). All limitations are accompanied by information on their source within the app.
  • Safety: HealthLens alerts users of changes and makes no diagnoses. The 3D body is an anatomy model from public atlases, never a photo of a person.

What tools did we use?

React, TypeScript, Vite; three.js for 3D rendering of the body (anatomy obtained from BodyParts3D and HuBMAP Human Reference Atlas using glTF Transform and meshoptimizer); OpenRouter with free open vision models (NVIDIA Nemotron, Google Gemma) for skin spot recognition; Zod for the response schema; SVG graphics; Vitest for the rules testing; Geist typography and Lucide icons; deployed to Vercel.

What's next?

Integrate the wearable and hardware devices through the existing device import mechanism, use the skin model on the tablet for scanning without requiring any connection, get real doctors to validate the guide and the skin rules through public dermatology pictures (ISIC), and automatically send the flight surgeon report through the next available communication window.
